transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-03-02
Start time: 14:30 PDT
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Rourke (Redwood SE), Zara Patel (Redwood CSM), Rajiv Menon (GreenForge Eng Lead), Helena Ortiz (GreenForge SRE), Darren Wu (GreenForge ML Infra), Sofia Abramson (GreenForge Product), Caller 5

Summary:
Quick sync on pilot throughput tuning (continuous batching behavior, concurrency targets, queue shaping) after last week's baseline runs. Main goals: confirm concurrency settings that meet 95th-tail latency SLO, validate queue shaping to avoid burst collapse, and plan next bench runs for production-like traffic.

Topics:
- Baseline results recap (tokens/sec, 50/95/99 latencies)
- Continuous batching thresholds and max batch size tradeoffs
- Concurrency target strategies (per-GPU vs per-model)
- Queueing/backpressure & graceful fallbacks
- Next steps and owner assignments

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: All right everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, then we'll jump into the numbers. How's everyone doing?
[00:07] Rajiv Menon: Good, thanks. Ready to dig in.
[00:09] Liam O'Rourke: Hey, hi all. I have the bench outputs up - I'll share screen in a sec.
[00:13] Helena Ortiz: Morning for me. Apologies if I sound echo-y, am on a hotspot.
[00:17] Maya Chen: No worries. Ok, Liam, baseline highlights?
[00:21] Liam O'Rourke: Yeah. So last Tuesday we ran three variants: conservative batching (max batch 8, batch window 12ms), default continuous batching (max 32, window adaptive), and aggressive (max 64 with 40ms window). For GreenForge model mix (avg request length ~220 tokens), conservative gave us steady latency 50th at 60ms, 95th at 220ms, 99th at 440ms; default was 50/90/220 - sorry, 50th 45ms, 95th 150ms, 99th 320ms; aggressive dropped avg tokens/sec by 28% because of queueing head-of-line stalls on bursts, 95th spiked to 560ms.
[00:50] Rajiv Menon: Wait, aggressive dropped throughput? I thought bigger batches = better throughput.
[00:55] Liam O'Rourke: Right, normally. But because your traffic has sudden spikes (short TTL bursts), we hit queueing collapse: large batches wait for slow arrivals, then the GPU idles while waiting for more requests, so effective throughput suffers. Also we saw larger kv-cache churn on these long prompts which increased end-to-end time.
[01:12] Darren Wu: kv-cache churn, that's the K V cache? Transcriptiontag, sorry.
[01:16] Maya Chen: Yeah, KV cache — occasionally shows up as K V in transcripts. The point is cache re-use patterns changed with batching.
[01:20] Sofia Abramson: Can we tune so that large batches happen only on steady tails, not during spikes?
[01:25] Liam O'Rourke: Exactly. Redwood's continuous batching supports adaptive thresholds: grow batch when inter-arrival time averages below X and shrink when queue latency exceeds Y. We recommend a dual-threshold: target batch size of 24 but with a soft cap at 40, and a backlog timer of 18ms so you don't wait too long. That gave the best 95th balance.
[01:42] Helena Ortiz: For our SLOs we need 95th under 200ms for chat flows and 99th under 500ms for async generation. Does the recommended settings meet that consistently?
[01:51] Liam O'Rourke: In bench #2 (the adaptive one) we hit 95th of ~150ms for the mix and 99th ~320ms, which meets chat SLO for 95th but 99th is tight vs async goal. There are two levers: reduce concurrency or enable prefix caching for long prompts. Prefix caching dropped 99th to ~260ms in an extra run.
[02:12] Rajiv Menon: What about concurrency? We currently shard model execution across 4 GPUs, but we run 40 containers total. We need guidance on per-GPU concurrency so we don't swamp memory.
[02:22] Liam O'Rourke: For the model you're using (7B-ish family, quantized), our sweet spot per GPU was 6 concurrent streams with batching target 24. Higher concurrency (10-12) improved throughput slightly but raised 99th tail. Memory pressure also rose, especially during mixed-length requests.
[02:39] Maya Chen: Right, and remember Dedicated vs Hosted matters — on Dedicated you get predictable GPU pool, so hitting per-GPU concurrency is straightforward. On Hosted, there's more routing jitter.
[02:48] Sofia Abramson: We're leaning Dedicated for pilot, yes.
[02:50] Helena Ortiz: On the network side, when you say routing jitter, is that about cross-AZ hops? We have egress limits that might throttle bursts.
[02:58] Liam O'Rourke: Cross-AZ increases tail a bit; we instrumented tails by region. For bursts, you want queue shaping at the LB and request-level admission controls. Redwood has rate-shaping knobs and can do graceful fallback to a smaller quantized variant if queue latency goes above threshold.
[03:15] Rajiv Menon: How does graceful fallback affect output quality? We can't afford lower-quality hallucinations for certain flows.
[03:21] Maya Chen: Good point. Fallback is policy-driven: for non-critical async tasks, you can accept a smaller model; for chat SLO-critical traffic we can instead route to reserved capacity or slow the client. We'll help create routing policies that map endpoints to strategies.
[03:36] Darren Wu: On telemetry — can you export per-request timings? We need the full breakdown: pre-queue, queue, batch assembly, kernel time, post-process.
[03:44] Liam O'Rourke: Yes. We can add per-request spans; in bench outputs you'll see per-stage timers. I'll include a CSV with columns for those spans.
[03:52] Sofia Abramson: Great. Can you also add an end-to-end synthetic that mimics our bursty traffic (Poisson tail + scheduled spikes)?
[03:58] Liam O'Rourke: Yep, we ran a synthetic called 'burst-sim-v2' that uses a heavy-tailed inter-arrival. I'll extend it to match your 95th% spike amplitude if you share the real traces.
[04:09] Rajiv Menon: We'll share traces. Also, one weird observation: on bench runs we saw occasional 1-second transients even on the adaptive config. Any idea what caused that?
[04:18] Liam O'Rourke: Two suspects: garbage collection in the host (python workers) and occasional model swap at kernel level when the batch window crosses a size that triggers a different kernel path. We're investigating. Adding warm-up padding and sticking to steady batch windows reduced those events.
[04:32] Helena Ortiz: Ok. About the bench CSVs you mentioned — will they show per-worker CPU and GPU utilization?
[04:38] Liam O'Rourke: Yes, per-process CPU, GPU utilization, PCIe transfer spikes, and mem usage. That helped us see that some stalls were due to host-side IO spikes.
[04:47] Maya Chen: Practical question — what should GreenForge change in config today before next run to get clearer signals?
[04:53] Liam O'Rourke: I recommend: cap max_batch to 40, soft target 24, backlog_timer 18ms, concurrency 6 per GPU, enable prefix caching for long-context flows, and enable per-endpoint routing so chat endpoints get reserved headroom. Also set the queue admission to drop requests that exceed 250ms queue time optionally (or route them to background).
[05:12] Rajiv Menon: If we drop requests at 250ms queue time, do you have client-retry guidance? We don't want client storms.
[05:19] Liam O'Rourke: Use exponential backoff with jitter, and prefer client-side hedging for idempotent calls. For chat flows avoid aggressive retries — instead route to reserved capacity or show degraded UI.
[05:29] Sofia Abramson: For product, showing a short 'thinking' indicator while waiting 200-300ms might be fine.
[05:33] Maya Chen: Ok, I'm going to mark the next steps. But first, any blockers we didn't cover?
[05:37] Helena Ortiz: Security check — we need to confirm KMS integration details for Dedicated pilot. Who's the contact?
[05:43] Maya Chen: Zara will own that. Zara, can you confirm KMS/HSM integration guide and the SOC2 artifact?
[05:48] Zara Patel: Yes, I'll send the KMS runbook and SOC2 summary and pointer to the audit logs doc. Expect it by EOD tomorrow.
[05:55] Rajiv Menon: Perfect.
[05:57] Maya Chen: Ok action items then: Liam will upload detailed bench CSVs, Maya to kick off targeted runs and share a bench spreadsheet, Rajiv to send traffic traces, Zara to send security artifacts, Helena to confirm network constraints. We'll reconvene after bench results.
[06:12] Darren Wu: Quick question on measurement: you reported 95th at 150ms — is that server-side only or includes network?
[06:18] Liam O'Rourke: Those numbers are server-side process times (pre-queue through post process). We can add synthetic network hops to estimate client-perceived latency.
[06:25] Sofia Abramson: Can Redwood include an A/B of prefix caching vs full context for a sample of our top 100 prompts?
[06:32] Liam O'Rourke: Yes, we'll run that as part of the bench matrix.
[06:35] Maya Chen: Time check — 5 minutes left. Any final clarifications?
[06:39] Rajiv Menon: One ask: can we get an ops playbook with recommended alarms (CPU, queue depth, 95th token rate) and suggested thresholds?
[06:45] Zara Patel: We'll produce a short ops playbook aligned to the bench results.
[06:49] Maya Chen: Great. OK last recap — I'll write the summary in the meeting notes and include the bench matrix. Expect bench CSVs and an initial ops playbook by Friday.
[06:58] Helena Ortiz: Thanks all.
[07:00] Maya Chen: Thanks team, talk soon.

Recap & explicit next steps:
- Redwood to run three targeted bench runs (conservative/adaptive/targeted burst) and upload full CSVs + per-stage spans - owner: Maya & Liam - due 2027-03-05
- GreenForge to provide 7-day production QPS/arrival trace and request length distribution - owner: Rajiv - due 2027-03-04
- Zara (Redwood CSM) to send KMS integration guide and SOC2 summary - due 2027-03-03
